| `prowler` | `rds_instance_no_public_access` | `nr-db` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(i), NIS2 Art.21(2)(g), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.13, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 6.7, ISO27001:2022 A.8.20 |  | guidance only | No code is generated because the instance is not in your Terraform state, and clients that connect over the internet lose access at once. Find who connects first (VPC flow logs, aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier DB). Then run: aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier DB --no-publicly-accessible --apply-immediately. If the instance is in your Terraform code, set publicly_accessible = false on aws_db_instance instead, or the next apply turns it on again. Also remove 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 from the security group on the database port. |
| `prowler` | `rds_instance_backup_enabled` | `nr-db` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(c), DORA Art.12, ISO27001:2022 A.8.13 |  | guidance only | No code is generated because the instance is not in your Terraform state. Turn on backups: aws rds modify-db-instance --db-instance-identifier DB --backup-retention-period DAYS --apply-immediately. Pick DAYS (1 to 35) from your recovery point objective. If the instance is in your Terraform code, set backup_retention_period on aws_db_instance instead, or the next apply turns backups off again. Turning backups on can cause a short I/O pause on a single-AZ instance, and it is charged by storage. Test a restore after the first backup exists. |

| `prowler` | `ec2_ebs_public_snapshot` | `snap-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(i), NIS2 Art.21(2)(g), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.21, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 11.1, ISO27001:2022 A.8.3 |  | guidance only | No code is generated because snapshots are not managed by Terraform. Make the snapshot private: aws ec2 modify-snapshot-attribute --snapshot-id SNAP --attribute createVolumePermission --operation-type remove --group-names all. Share it with named accounts only (--user-ids). Anyone may have copied the data already: check CloudTrail and rotate any secret on the volume. To stop it from happening again, turn on EBS snapshot block public access (ec2_ebs_snapshot_account_block_public_access). |
| `prowler` | `ec2_ebs_snapshots_encrypted` | `snap-0f0e0d0c0b0a09080` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(h), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.6, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 9.1, ISO27001:2022 A.8.24 |  | guidance only | No code is generated: an existing snapshot cannot be encrypted in place. Copy it with encryption: aws ec2 copy-snapshot --source-region REGION --source-snapshot-id SNAP --encrypted --kms-key-id KEY. Use the new snapshot from now on and delete the old one when nothing needs it. A snapshot shared with other accounts needs a customer-managed key those accounts may use. Turn on EBS default encryption (ec2_ebs_default_encryption) so new snapshots are encrypted. |
| `prowler` | `awslambda_function_url_public` | `nr-fn` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(i), NIS2 Art.21(2)(g), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.21, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 11.1, ISO27001:2022 A.5.15 |  | guidance only | No code is generated because the function is not in your Terraform state, and callers without AWS credentials lose access at once. Find who calls the URL first. Then run: aws lambda update-function-url-config --function-name FUNCTION --auth-type AWS_IAM. Grant lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl only to the principals that need it. If the URL is in your Terraform code, set authorization_type = "AWS_IAM" on aws_lambda_function_url instead. If the function must be public, put a gateway with its own authentication in front, or delete the URL: aws lambda delete-function-url-config --function-name FUNCTION. |
| `prowler` | `awslambda_function_not_publicly_accessible` | `nr-fn` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(i), NIS2 Art.21(2)(g), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.21, NIS2 CIR 2024/2690 Annex 11.1, ISO27001:2022 A.5.15 |  | guidance only | No code is generated because the policy statement is not in your Terraform state, and callers lose access at once. List the statements: aws lambda get-policy --function-name FUNCTION. Remove the one with Principal "\*": aws lambda remove-permission --function-name FUNCTION --statement-id SID. Add a statement for the real caller, with its fixed ARN or service principal and a source ARN or source account condition: aws lambda add-permission --function-name FUNCTION --statement-id NEW_SID --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal PRINCIPAL --source-arn SOURCE_ARN. If the permission is in your Terraform code, change aws_lambda_permission there instead. |
| `prowler` | `awslambda_function_using_supported_runtimes` | `nr-fn` | NIS2 Art.21(2)(e), DORA Art.9, DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art.10, ISO27001:2022 A.8.8 |  | guidance only | No code is generated: a newer runtime can break the function code and its dependencies, so it needs a test. Pick a supported runtime from the Lambda runtimes page of the AWS documentation. Update a copy first: publish a version, test it behind an alias, then move the alias. Then run: aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name FUNCTION --runtime RUNTIME. If the function is in your Terraform code, set runtime on aws_lambda_function instead, or the next apply sets the old one again. Rebuild layers and native dependencies for the new runtime. |
